extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/aesthetics interested in the nature of laughter and the ludicrous
extracted.subtask_description: Explicates a philosophical theory of the ludicrous: the psychological source of laughter, distinctions among types of the ludicrous (wit, folly, pun), and related phenomena (pedantry, jester/clown technique). Useful for analyzing or composing humorous effects from an incongruity perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of laughter (incongruity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of laughter in every case is simply the sudden perception of the incongruity between a concept and the real objects which have been thought through it in some relation, and laughter itself is just the expression of this incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sudden perception is essential; the ludicrous arises when a concept that seemed applicable is revealed as inadequate by contrast with reality. This is the central explanatory principle for all examples of the ludicrous; no further anecdotes are necessary to confirm it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two species of the ludicrous: wit and folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Either we have previously known two or more very different real objects and have intentionally identified them through the unity of a concept (wit), or the concept is first present and we pass from it to reality resulting in foolish action (folly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit: intentional, typically verbal, uniting disparate objects under one concept. Folly: unintentional, generally exhibited in action when a concept is misapplied to different objects. Distinguish by whether the identification was deliberate (wit) or an outwardly performed misapplication (folly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit: method and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit always shows itself in words (when not disguised as folly); it consists in intentionally bringing two very different real objects under one concept so that their other differences produce surprise and ludicrous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make wit: deliberately subsume unlike items under a single concept and reveal the mismatch. Witticisms are verbal and intentional—craft and timing are crucial. The jester may mask wit as folly for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly: method and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Folly results when a concept is applied in action to objects which are fundamentally different but treated the same, leading to surprise when their other aspects appear; generally unintentional and external.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Folly is primarily an action-based comic device; it may appear in words when intentions are expressed without execution. Comedic effect depends on the actor's unawareness and the audience's perception of the mismatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of ludicrous relates to correctness and contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: The more correct the subsumption of objects under a concept from one point of view, and the greater and more glaring their incongruity with that concept from another point of view, the greater is the ludicrous effect produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comic situations balance a plausible shared feature (so subsumption seems correct) against a striking dissimilarity elsewhere. Stronger paradox/unexpected contrast yields stronger laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jester/clown technique: concealing wit as folly
rubrics_metrics.description: To seem to reverse the starting-point and to conceal wit with the mask of folly is the art of the jester and the clown: being aware of the diversity of objects, the jester unites them under one concept and then, starting from that concept, causes the subsequent discovery of diversity to surprise the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique uses the audience's perception of intentionality and performance—presenting an apparent foolish action that is actually an orchestrated wit. It's an important performance strategy for comic actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedantry as a comic source (anti-pattern for correct judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedantry is a form of folly arising from lack of confidence in one’s understanding and excessive reliance on abstract concepts, rules and maxims; the pedant applies general concepts where fine distinctions of the concrete are required, producing awkwardness and ludicrous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pedantry as comedic character: rigid adherence to form or general maxims in situations demanding sensitivity produces comic mismatch. Anti-pattern: overuse makes humor predictable or merely didactic rather than genuinely ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pun (calembourg) as a spurious, superficial wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The pun brings two different concepts, by the assistance of accident, under one word: it is a play upon words where difference lies in the concepts and identity lies in the reality (terminology), hence more familiar and more superficial than genuine witticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns rely on accidental nomenclature equivalences; they are a lighter, more superficial form of wit. They produce a familiar kind of laugh and are often used for bawdy or obscene double entendre. They may be unintentional (misunderstanding) or intentional; the former resembles folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of expression: words vs actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit must always show itself in words (except when disguised), while folly generally shows itself in actions, though it can appear in words when it expresses an intention without execution or in judgments and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing humor, choose verbal forms for witty paradoxes and performative situations for folly. Mixing modes (verbal folly, acted wit) can create hybrid effects but risks diluting clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness and paradox are essential to the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: All laughter is occasioned by a paradox, and therefore by unexpected subsumption, whether expressed in words or actions; the ludicrous requires an element of surprise and an apparent contradiction between expectation (concept) and reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing and the element of surprise are vital; build an expectation from a concept and then reveal the contradictory reality. Without suddenness, the incongruity loses its comic force.
